sources.note: Contributed the AI-tell catalog. Filtered from 37 patterns to the ~21 that fire in a technical register and compressed to one-line rows.
Contributed the composition rules. Strunk's 18 rules condensed to the 8 that apply to short technical prose. The elements-of-style reference files were dropped.

modifications: Authoring-first, not editing-first: humanizer's draft/audit/final rewrite loop, travel-blog example, DETECTION GUIDANCE, and PERSONALITY AND SOUL sections were dropped.
Scope narrowed to repo and forge prose. Voiced and long-form prose stays with humanizer.
Dropped curly-quote pattern (Claude emits straight ASCII) and the Wikipedia-article framing of the significance, notability, and challenges patterns.

Added a content rule (carry why, not what), length-and-silence rules, git-shaped worked examples, guidance for error messages, log lines, and code comments, and anti-patterns specific to agent-written git prose. None of these exist upstream.
Inverted upstream's diff-anchored-writing rule for commits, changelogs, and migration guides, where narrating the change is correct.
DO NOT TOUCH condensed to five lines and extended to identifiers, CLI flags, and file paths.
Renamed from repo-prose to oss-writing on migration into oss-kit.
Split into a core and one reference file. The tell catalog moved to references/tells.md and loads only when a draft is suspect, per R-SKL-07; the core keeps a single link to it.

Added four composition rules paraphrased from ASD-STE100 Issue 9 (name the referent, cap noun stacks at three, one instruction per step, keep the articles), and its sentence, paragraph, and noun-stack figures as limits: under 20 words in an instruction, under 25 in an explanation, under six sentences in a paragraph. They were stated as signals to split rather than limits until a skill change measured that a signal does not bind. ASD-STE100 is copyright ASD and an EU registered trademark. No rule text, dictionary entry, or other wording was copied from it; the rules were written from its principles and it is cited by name. Its approved-word dictionary and no-gerund rule were rejected as a poor fit for software prose. Its rule against omitting a verb, subject, or article to shorten text is why the keep-the-articles rule survives a pass aimed at brevity.
Added a normative statements section for the RFC 2119 and RFC 8174 uppercase keywords.

Attached a reason to every hard constraint and moved the worked examples into <example> tags, following Anthropic's Claude 5 context engineering post, the Opus 5 prompting page, and the prompting best practices page.

Added a nominalized gerund chain row to the catalog. Prefer-the-common-word folded into the AI-vocabulary row and synonym drift into elegant variation, because both already existed there under other names.
Dropped the duplicate commit-body example and shortened the bad half of each remaining pair.

Replaced the per-artifact content table for commits and change requests with one length ladder: the body defaults to none and exists only on one of six named triggers. The table listed what a body carries and read as a checklist to cover. A template's required sections still win over the ladder, which decides how much each one gets rather than whether it appears.

Split the GitHub and GitLab render mechanics into references/forge-rendering.md, loaded only at the branch that needs it, per R-SKL-07. The body keeps one forge-agnostic wrapping rule. Nothing upstream has this content.

Replaced the bad-and-good example pairs for git prose with finished artifacts at each rung, each named for the trigger that earned its body. The bad halves demonstrated the padded output the skill was still producing, so the recognition half was not working. Pairs stay in references/tells.md, where the contrast is the lesson.
Narrowed the ban on working-process narration to the author's route to the fix. Naming the failure a change targets is a reproduction, which Git's SubmittingPatches requires of a commit body.

Added a hard constraint against a clause that tells the reader how to weigh a fact just stated. Upstream's closer patterns are promotional; the defensive form is not upbeat, carries none of the significance-inflation vocabulary, and passes the sentence-length caps, so nothing already in the skill fired on it.

Rebuilt the body from the cited sources, which were re-read on 2026-07-28, rather than trimmed. Each source was distilled and then filtered against Anthropic's skill-authoring criterion, that a skill should only add context the model does not already have. Most of what the sources say fails that filter and was cut: imperative mood, the 50-character subject, small focused change requests, second person, active voice as a bare instruction, and Conventional Commits in full, which is a 2019 standard the model knows and which a repository declares for itself. What survived is what changes the output. From Git's SubmittingPatches: the three-part body order, the status quo in the present tense, self-containment over a link, splitting a change whose description runs long, and 'git show -s --pretty=reference' for citing a prior commit. From GitHub's review guidance: naming where to start reading, and the shape of a review comment. From the Google developer documentation style guide, used under CC BY 4.0: the timeless-language word list, the ban on inflecting a code element, and putting a condition before its instruction. Body went from 203 lines to 147.

Dropped the RFC 2119 section, the per-artifact content table covering issues and ADRs, and the six-bullet body-trigger ladder. The first two restate what the model already produces on request; the ladder read as a checklist to satisfy, and Git's three-part body says the same thing better and with an authority behind it.

Removed references/forge-rendering.md and the squash-reuse warning it supported, which is a capability loss rather than a relocation. It said that a forge can be configured to turn a change-request description into the permanent commit message, that no clone reveals the setting, and that GitHub rewraps the body at roughly 76 columns. That is per-forge mechanics, too specific to earn lines that load on every invocation. The one clause that changes what gets typed survives in the core: keep the subject under 72 characters, counting any number the forge appends on squash.

Scoped the timeless-language rule to documentation, and named commits, change-request descriptions, changelog entries, and migration guides as the exception. A three-arm evaluation caught this: the first draft of the rule carved out only changelog entries, so the arm running it wrote a pull request description that avoided the word 'now' where 'now' was correct, since describing a change is what that artifact is for. references/tells.md already carried the wider carve-out on its diff-anchored row, so the core and the reference disagreed.

Replaced the ad-hoc hedging-stack row with a simple-verb-forms composition rule paraphrased from ASD-STE100, which is the principled version of it, and folded the global-and-accessible-prose section into one composition row. Public secondary material on ASD-STE100 was read on 2026-07-28 to confirm the figures the skill already carried on trust. The specification itself is paywalled and was not read, and no wording from it is reproduced.

Ported three things from an independently researched skill draft that was evaluated against this one: a rule-to-checker map in references/linting.md, a flattened banned-word list for a substitution linter, and Conventional Comments labels as an option for a repository that has adopted them. All three land in references or as one conditional clause, not in the always-loaded body. A four-arm blind evaluation, twenty-four judgements over two rounds with the outputs shuffled and the judges shown no skill, is what decided that placement: a fused variant that merged both rule sets into its core scored 100 percent on every mechanical check and placed last on judged quality, never once first, because stacked sentence caps and one-instruction-per-sentence fragment the prose. This skill scored 28 Borda in both rounds, before and after the port, so the additions cost nothing in judged quality.

Extended the change-request guidance after blind judging put this skill last on that artifact in eight straight judgements across two rounds, while it placed first on commits and review comments. Judges named three faults every time: changed files missing from the summary, a template section asking for something beyond CI answered by listing the CI checks, and a disclosed gap left with no way to close it. The fix is coverage and comprehension rather than length, and it keeps the ban on a bullet per file, so the terseness default still holds everywhere else. A third round scored 30 Borda against 28 before, with the change-request prompt moving from last to second.

Sharpened the consequence condition after a 100-prompt evaluation found this skill placing last on trivial-looking commits. The diagnosis needed three passes and two of them were wrong. The first blamed the prompts, which did carry safety facts the stratum was supposed to exclude. The second blamed the prompt format, which did leak the stratum name to the model, though stripping it changed nothing for this skill. The third found the real fault by testing the skill against clean prompts: it suppressed a body whenever the diff looked small, regardless of whether the facts earned one. Two clauses fix it, one saying the consequence condition reaches a change whose safety rests on a fact the diff cannot show, one saying the size of the change does not decide. Measured unlabelled on 59 tasks, the skill moved from 0 of 7 earned bodies to 7 of 7 while still writing none of the 27 unearned. An unaided model scores 56 of 59 on the same set, writing two bodies that are not earned.

Cut three bullets from the core rule list as duplicates. Coordinate ideas in similar form is the parallel-form rule a few lines above it. Sentence case and the dash ban both survive in the check list, where they carry a reason and run before a draft is returned. A wider trim was tried and reverted: twelve more bullets were cut on the ground that a model already produces them, which is an assumption about every model any host runs this skill on rather than a finding, and no evaluation in this repository settles it. Restoring them costs twelve lines in a body under a hundred, against an unmeasured quality loss on a model nobody has tested, so the list stays long. Two improvements from that pass were kept: the positive-form rule regained the carve-out that a negative stays where prohibition is the point, and the concrete-words rule gained the example that makes it act. The six grammar rules also gained the terminal periods and the expanded 'do not' the rest of the list uses, which its own parallel-form rule requires.

Restored the sentence-count step to the check list, where the split into per-artifact references had dropped it. The caps sit in the core rule list and references/linting.md ranks sentence length first among the rules a checker can decide, but the list a model reads before returning a draft had no step for it. It is the only rule in the skill that needs counting rather than recognizing, so it goes first, while a reader working down the list is still willing to edit. The wording is the one measured earlier: it took the worst prompt from four over-length sentences to one and the Opus arm from 98 to 99 percent.

Brought the skill's own prose under the 25-word cap it asks a reader to count first. Twelve sentences ran long, eight of them inside the check list itself, where the counting step now sits at the top. Each split follows the shape the step names: a rule, a colon, then a reason joined by 'and' or 'so', so the colon became a period. The Redis paragraph in the worked commit body was split too, because an example that breaches the cap teaches the breach. The frontmatter description stays at 33 words, as trigger text a host matches rather than prose a reader reads.

Deleted the default pull request skeleton from references/commits-and-prs.md. It invented scaffolding for a repository that ships no template, where the skill already says to follow the conventions and templates the repository declares. Its Changes section listed one bullet per change, which the same file forbids two sections above as restating the diff, and its headings would land in git log on a squash merge. Settled on one name for the artifact while removing it, since the file had called it both a PR and a pull request. The frontmatter keeps PR, which is what a user types when asking for one.

Scoped the review-comment rules that contradicted each other in references/code-review.md. One line told a reviewer to state the problem and let the author choose the fix, while two others told them to give the required outcome and to pair every issue with a suggestion. Both halves are load-bearing, so neither was dropped: the fix is supplied where exactly one edit is right, and the choice is left to the author where several are. The pairing rule now carries the same condition.

Closed the sentence-cap escape hatch that references/docs-and-readme.md had opened, which let narrative prose relax the one rule the check list asks a reader to count. It arrived with the split into per-artifact references and no measurement, and half of it restated the core cap rather than relaxing it. Cut three bullets from the same file as second copies of core rules, keeping the worked example one of them carried by moving it up to the rule itself. Removing a duplicate from a reference is safe where removing a rule from the body is not, because the body is read before any reference is.

Dropped the guidance for error messages, log lines, and code comments that the entry above records adding. Those strings live inside source files, so covering them would put this kit in the business of editing code, which is not what it is for. The frontmatter description no longer claims them. Dropped the rule that a change request description account for every changed file, which came from a judge panel rather than a source: the reviewer already has the file list, and restating it is the noise this skill bans one section above. What a reader needs is a reason for a file the subject does not imply, and that is not the same rule. Settled on 'change request' for the artifact, after a first pass standardized on GitHub's 'pull request' in a skill whose forge scope is GitHub and GitLab. references/commits-and-prs.md is renamed to references/commits-and-change-requests.md to match.

Settled four small faults in the body. Two example headings carried a note explaining why the example exists, which is a message to this file's author rather than its reader, and one rule pointed at a heading the reader reaches anyway. The opening ran three fragments in a row, the run of short declaratives references/tells.md names as manufactured drama, and one of them restated the terseness the next one states better. The agent-facing trigger asked for the core rules 'at full strictness', which implies they apply partially elsewhere, so it now names the tighter cap it actually wants. One boundary had three names, procedural sentence in the rule and numbered step in the check, so both now say instruction. references/linting.md keeps numbered step, because a checker can find one and cannot tell an instruction from a description.
